relationship: Contrast in the possibility of an answer
rationale: Job anticipates a divine refusal to listen that prevents an answer to even one word out of a thousand. After actually hearing the Lord, he later asks what answer he can give, covers his mouth and says he will add nothing. The comparison distinguishes the earlier denied hearing from his later inability to answer.

Job says the righteous are mocked, then describes a righteous and blameless man becoming an object of mockery. The later line expands the description with blamelessness while repeating the complaint about mockery of the righteous.

Job contrasts his cry of alas if ungodly with inability to look up even if righteous. Earlier he feared that even righteousness and blamelessness would end with an impious mouth and a crooked result. Both express his sense that innocence does not secure a fair outcome.

Job describes being hunted like a lion for slaughter. Lamentations portrays the divine adversary as a hidden lion who pursues and desolates the speaker. Both employ predation imagery for affliction, but Job is the hunted comparison while the lament describes the pursuer.

relationship: Water and plant survival in opposing speeches
rationale: Job describes water bringing renewed growth even when the root grows old and the trunk dies in rock. Bildad had asked whether papyrus or rushes flourish without water and described unwatered plants withering. Their plant images agree about dependence on water but place it within different arguments about hope.

relationship: Shared drinking metaphor: injustice and mockery
rationale: Eliphaz describes an unclean man drinking injustice like a drink. Elihu later describes Job as drinking mockery like water. The comparison concerns the distinctive drinking metaphor, while injustice and mockery and the speakers' applications remain distinct.

relationship: The ungodly person's wealth failing to endure
rationale: Eliphaz says the ungodly person's belongings will not remain. Proverbs says property eagerly pursued with lawlessness becomes less, contrasting it with pious increase. Both connect wealth's failure to a negative moral description, but only Proverbs here specifies the manner of acquisition; neither comparison proves Job's former wealth unjust.

relationship: Recurring image: divine arrows in Job
rationale: Job describes anger and the arrows of God's raiders falling upon him, returning to his earlier statement that the Lord's arrows are in his body and stab him when he speaks. Both portray suffering as an armed divine assault from Job's perspective, without identifying every raider.

Job says strangers stole his belongings. The opening reports describe raiders carrying off oxen and donkeys and horsemen carrying off camels. These losses give narrative context to the complaint without assigning an ethnicity to the unnamed strangers.

relationship: Recurring cosmic imagery: sea creatures subject to God
rationale: Job says the sea creatures under heaven bent beneath God. Later he credits God with calming the sea, wounding the great sea creature and killing the rebellious dragon. The lines share divine mastery over the sea and its great creatures, without equating every creature or action.
